title: Advent: the prophets' candle
hook: the first candle recalls the prophets who hoped

segments.voice: Yesterday, dies natalis: a saint's day of death, kept as a birthday into heaven. Your line was a birthday into heaven.

"The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light." Somebody reads that line in a dim church, or at a kitchen table after supper, and then strikes a match. In front of them is a ring of greenery with candles set in it. Only one gets lit. The others wait their turn, one more each Sunday, until the waiting is over. It's a small flame for such a big sentence, and that's the point. For churches that keep this calendar, the year begins here, with a season called Advent, and a candle for people who hoped.

Advent is the church's word for a coming. It names the weeks before Christmas, when Christians remember the waiting for Christ's birth and, they say, wait again for him to come at the end of time. Catholics, Anglicans, Lutherans, Methodists and others keep it with readings and candles; Orthodox Christians keep their own season of fasting before the Nativity; some churches don't mark it at all. Churches name the first candle differently: some call it the prophets' candle, others the candle of hope. It comes to the same place. The prophets hoped for what they could not see. Isaiah spoke to a land that knew war and fear, and promised: "The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light: they that dwell in the land of the shadow of death, upon them hath the light shined." A few verses on: "For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given." Christians read that child as Christ; Isaiah himself does not live to see him. Matthew tells of Jesus beginning to preach in Galilee, and reaches back for the same words: "The people which sat in darkness saw great light." Jews read Isaiah's promise in their own way, and that reading is theirs to tell. For Christians, the first candle stands for all that waiting. Paul puts it plainly: "hope that is seen is not hope: for what a man seeth, why doth he yet hope for?" Hope lives in the dark, or it isn't hope.

segments.voice: Light one candle, or turn the room lights down and use any small light you have, and read the line slowly: the people that walked in darkness have seen a great light. Watch the flame, and let something you're waiting for sit beside it, without pushing it to arrive. If you pray, you can pray Isaiah's line back to God; if you don't, simply keep watching the light.
Advent. The weeks of waiting before Christmas, for a coming. Its first candle, in some churches, remembers the prophets who hoped for a light they did not see.
Your line: hope. One flame lit, the rest still waiting. Day one thousand three.

chat.says: What's the deal with lighting just one candle on that wreath?
options: It's Advent: one candle for the prophets' hope, then one more each Sunday till Christmas.
It's for Christmas itself: each candle stands for one of the twelve days.
Each candle honors one saint, and the first is for that Sunday's saint.
chat.meaning: Advent's first candle, called the prophets' candle or the candle of hope, stands for waiting. One more is lit each Sunday until the waiting is over.

notes: Claims rule: no number of candles, Sundays or weeks is stated; no date for the wreath's origin.

Who keeps Advent: Catholics, Anglicans, Lutherans, Methodists and others; Orthodox keep the Nativity Fast; some churches don't mark it. Confirm fair and unranked.
Candle names vary by church and resource (prophecy/prophets' candle, hope); the script says so. Colors are not mentioned here because Gaudete (day 1005) covers the rose candle.
